SYSTEMIC ISSUE SUMMARY PayPal maintains exclusive control over billing authorization tokens used to debit consumer accounts. These tokens : Persist after subscription cancellation, Persist after refunds acknowledging lack of authorization or service, Persist after explicit consumer notice to stop payment, Can not be viewed, revoked, or XXXX by consumers. 

XXXXayPals system allows continued withdrawals without consumer control and without merchant-visible billing artifacts.

OBSERVABLE SYSTEM BEHAVIOR Across affected accounts, PayPal transaction histories display : Debit entries labeled as withdrawals, No invoice records, No subscription records, No contemporaneous merchant billing requests, No settlement or remittance confirmation to merchants.

The only verifiable action is that PayPal debits the consumer account. PayPal does not provide a c
onsumer-accessible audit trail establishing that : A merchant initiated the charge at the time of debit, or Funds were transferred to a merchant rather than retained internally.

REGULATORY IMPLICATIONS ( SYSTEMIC ) This practice implicates multiple provisions of the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E ( 12 CFR Part 1005 ) on a systemic basis, including : Unauthorized electronic fund transfers ( 1005.2 ( m ) ), Failure to honor stop-payment instructions for preauthorized transfers ( 1005.10 ( c ) ), Failure to investigate and correct errors ( 1005.11 ).

PayPals token architecture prevents consumers from exercising statutory rights by design.

CONTROL AND AUTHORITY STRUCTURE PayPal, not merchants and not consumers, controls : Token issuance, Token persistence, Token execution, Token termination.

Consumers can not independently revoke authorization.

Stop-payment notices do not reliably terminate token execution.

Refunds do not permanently revoke tokens.

This places PayPal in the position of effective initiator of the transfer once merchant access is severed.

CONSUMER HARM ( CLASS-WIDE ) The system produces predictable harm : Unauthorized debits after cancellation or refund, Inability to stop payment through ordinary means, Forced card cancellation as a substitute for compliance, Loss of access to funds, Repeated withdrawals without transparent justification.

This harm is structural, not accidental.

REQUESTED CFPB ACTION ( SYSTEMIC ) I respectfully request that the CFPB : Investigate PayPals billing authorization token system as a systemic practice.

Require PayPal to demonstrate, for token-based withdrawals : Merchant-initiated billing requests, Settlement or remittance records to merchants.

Documentation demonstrating the described system behavior can be provided upon request.

Issue: Attempts to collect debt not owed

I did not open, authorize, apply for, sign for, or benefit from any account with Credit Collection, nor did I enter into any agreement that would create a legal obligation between myself and this company.

Because I have never had a contractual relationship with Credit Collection or the alleged original creditor, I immediately suspected that this account was the result of identity theft or fraudulent activity. 

Upon discovering this unauthorized account, I took prompt and reasonable steps to protect myself and address the situation. I filed an Identity Theft Report with the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC ), documenting that this account was opened fraudulently and without my knowledge or consent. Filing an FTC Identity Theft Report is a formal declaration under federal law that the account does not belong to me and that I am a victim of identity theft. 

In addition to filing the FTC report, I disputed the Credit Collection account with the consumer reporting agencies. In my disputes, I clearly stated that I do not own the account, that the account was opened fraudulently, and that I am not legally responsible for any alleged balance. I requested that Credit Collection provide lawful proof that I authorized the account, including a signed contract, application, billing statements showing my participation, or any documentation demonstrating that I agreed to the debt. 

Despite these actions, the Credit Collection tradeline has continued to appear on my credit report as a collection account. Continued reporting of this account has caused ongoing harm to my credit profile and financial standing. The presence of a collection account negatively impacts my creditworthiness, can affect my ability to obtain credit, housing, employment, and insurance, and creates stress and uncertainty as a victim of identity theft. 

Credit Collection has not provided independent or substantive proof that I opened or authorized this account. Simply asserting that a balance exists or relying on internal records or information received from another party does not establish that the account belongs to me. When an account is disputed as identity theft and an FTC Identity Theft Report has been filed, the burden is on the furnisher to verify that the account was legitimately opened and authorized by the consumer. To date, that burden has not been met. 

The continued reporting of this account is inaccurate and misleading. I am not the account holder, I did not incur the debt, and I have no legal obligation to Credit Collection. Reporting the account as a valid collection account falsely associates me with a debt that does not belong to me. This is especially concerning because victims of identity theft should not be required to repeatedly defend themselves against debts they did not create. 

I have acted in good faith throughout this process. I promptly reviewed my credit reports, identified the fraudulent account, filed the appropriate federal identity theft documentation, and disputed the account through the proper channels. I have cooperated fully and have taken all reasonable steps expected of a consumer in this situation. At this point, the continued presence of the Credit Collection account reflects a failure to correct inaccurate information rather than any inaction on my part. 

This matter is particularly troubling because collection accounts carry significant negative weight on a consumers credit report. The inaccurate reporting of a collection account can have long-lasting consequences that extend well beyond the balance allegedly owed. As a victim of identity theft, I should not be penalized for fraudulent activity committed by another party. 

I am also concerned that XXXX XXXX continued reporting XXXX rely on administrative handling rather than factual resolution. Closing a dispute or marking an account as verified without establishing lawful authorization does not convert fraudulent information into accurate information. If Credit Collection can not demonstrate that I opened or authorized this account, it should not continue to be reported or collected. 

I want to be clear that this complaint is not about dissatisfaction with customer service or a disagreement over billing. This complaint is about ownership of the account itself. I do not own this account. I never did. Any reporting, collection activity, or verification suggesting otherwise is incorrect. 

Because this account was opened fraudulently, it should not be sold, transferred, reassigned, or pursued by any third party. Any such actions would further propagate inaccurate information and compound the harm caused by the original identity theft. Credit Collection should ensure that its internal records clearly reflect that I am not the responsible party and that the account is associated with identity theft. 

I am submitting this complaint so that Credit Collection and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau can review the facts, recognize that this account does not belong to me, and ensure that my consumer credit reports reflect accurate information only. Victims of identity theft rely on accurate reporting and timely correction to restore their financial standing and protect themselves from further harm. 

In summary, the key facts are as follows : I do not own or recognize the Credit Collection account. 

I did not authorize, apply for, or benefit from the account. 

I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report documenting that the account is fraudulent. 

I disputed the account with the credit reporting agencies. 

Credit Collection has not provided lawful proof that I am the account holder. 

The account continues to be reported inaccurately as a collection account. 

Continued reporting causes ongoing harm to me as a consumer and identity theft victim. 

This complaint is submitted to request accountability, correction of inaccurate reporting, and appropriate handling of an identity theftrelated account. I respectfully request that Credit Collection review this matter thoroughly and take corrective action consistent with federal consumer protection laws and identity theft safeguards.

Issue: Dealing with your lender or servicer
Consumer complaint narrative:
I am the debtor and primary borrower on certain private student loan accounts serviced by Sallie Mae. 
I filed a voluntary petition for relief under XXXX XXXX of the Bankruptcy Code. An automatic stay pursuant to 11 U.S.C. 362 ( a ) became effective in XXXX and remained in effect until XX/XX/XXXX. ( see documentation below. ) Sallie Mae received notice of my bankruptcy filing and issued electronic communications acknowledging the bankruptcy and stating that no payment was due at that time. ( see documentation below. ) During the automatic stay, Sallie Mae restricted my access to my online borrower account, preventing me from viewing loan balances, payment status, correspondence, or notices. No physical mail regarding payment obligations or account status was sent to me during this period. 
While the automatic stay was in effect, Sallie Mae unilaterally altered its internal servicing designation by treating the cosigner as the primary borrower, despite the loan contract identifying me as the primary borrower. ( see documentation below. ) During the stay, Sallie Mae contacted the cosigner by telephone and electronic communications seeking payment on the loans. These communications occurred while Sallie Mae had knowledge of the bankruptcy filing and the automatic stay. 
The cosigner did not have an online account with Sallie Mae and did not select electronic delivery preferences. Sallie Mae nevertheless relied on electronic communication preferences selected by me to justify the absence of mailed notices, while sending electronic messages stating that documents were available online. 
After termination of the automatic stay, Sallie Mae reverted the borrower and cosigner designations to their original status and asserted that the loans were delinquent due to nonpayment during the automatic stay, demanding retroactive payment for that period. ( see documentation and recorded communication below ) Sallie Mae reported the loans as XXXX or more days past due to consumer reporting agencies beginning in XXXX, including periods when the automatic stay was in effect. ( see documentation below. ) Any alleged delinquency arose solely from XXXX XXXX conduct during the automatic stay and did not exist prior to the bankruptcy filing. 
XXXX XXXX actions caused emotional distress, significant time expenditure, and damage to my credit profile, and interfered with the fresh start protections afforded by the Bankruptcy Code.

Sallie Mae had actual notice of my Chapter 7 bankruptcy and the automatic stay imposed under 11 U.S.C. 362. Notwithstanding that notice, Sallie Mae engaged in conduct that includes, but is not limited to : ( 1 ) indirect collection activity during the automatic stay by reclassifying the cosigner as the primary borrower and contacting the cosigner for payment ; ( 2 ) restricting borrower access to account information while representing that no payment was due ; ( 3 ) retroactively assessing delinquency for the stay period ; and ( 4 ) furnishing inaccurate delinquency information to consumer reporting agencies.

Anticipated Company Position and Clarification 1. Internal Policies and Procedures Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may state that its internal policies and procedures were followed. 

Clarification : Internal policies and procedures do not supersede federal consumer protection laws applicable to private student loan lenders and servicers. Even where a company asserts compliance with its internal processes, the resulting conduct must still comply with : UDAAP prohibitions under 12 U.S.C. 5531 and 5536, FCRA accuracy and furnishing obligations under 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2, and Bankruptcy Code protections, including the automatic stay under 11 U.S.C. 362.

In this matter, Sallie Maes procedures resulted in the assessment of retroactive delinquency for a legally protected period, conflicting representations regarding payment obligations, and furnishing of misleading credit information. A servicing practice that produces outcomes inconsistent with federal law is not compliant, regardless of whether it aligns with internal policy. 

2. Credit Reporting Accuracy and Automation Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may assert that credit reporting is accurate, automated, or outside its control once furnished to consumer reporting agencies.

Clarification : Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, furnishersincluding private student loan lendersare responsible for ensuring the accuracy and completeness of information they provide to consumer reporting agencies. Reporting an account as delinquent for a period during which : payment was subject to a bankruptcy automatic stay, and the borrower was informed that no payment was due, is materially misleading. The use of automated systems does not relieve a furnisher of its statutory obligation to ensure that reported information accurately reflects the legal status of the account. 

3. Cosigner Liability and Collection Activity Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may contend that collection activity was permissible because a cosigner remained contractually liable.

Clarification : While a cosigner may remain liable under the loan contract, the conduct at issue exceeded permissible cosigner collection. During the bankruptcy period, Sallie Mae : internally altered borrower and cosigner designations without notice or authorization, relied on that alteration to maintain account activity during the automatic stay, and subsequently reversed the designation and carried forward delinquency to the primary borrower. 

This sequence reflects procedural handling that materially affected account status and post-bankruptcy delinquency, rather than ordinary cosigner collection activity, and directly contributed to retroactive payment demands and credit reporting harm. 

4. Repayment Programs and Upfront Payment Requirements Anticipated Position : Sallie Mae may state that repayment or assistance programs require financial review and an upfront payment before eligibility can be determined.

Clarification : While private student loan lenders may evaluate financial information, conditioning access to repayment options on an unspecified and undisclosed upfront payment, while refusing to disclose eligibility criteria or required amounts, raises concerns under XXXX. Withholding material information needed for a consumer to understand available options and obligations, while simultaneously demanding payment, constitutes unfair and potentially abusive servicing conduct. 

Purpose of This Clarification These clarifications are provided to ensure the CFPBs review focuses on the legal effect of XXXX XXXX servicing practices, rather than on whether internal policies were followed. The issues raised concern post-bankruptcy payment handling, credit reporting accuracy, and transparency, all of which are subject to federal consumer protection requirements for private student loan lenders.
